title: Hasidic Life and the Kloizn of Skala
summary: Skala’s distinct Hasidic groups and prayer houses show the variety of religious traditions within the community.
editorialContent:

## A town of many prayer houses

In [Skala](/communities/skala/records/mention_e45df50311765e6716832a1b), Hasidism was not a single congregation gathered around one local leader. It was a network of loyalties—to rebbes in nearby towns, to rabbis and teachers at home, and to the prayer houses where people met each day. The memorial book describes a town where Hasidism was deeply rooted, alongside a smaller number of non-Hasidic Jews and people less attached to the rebbes. It recalls about ten prayer and study houses and small synagogues, including the Chortkover, Vizhnitzer and Otynyer kloizn, as well as Itzik’s small prayer house and the “Port Arthur” synagogue.

The names point outward as well as inward. Chortkover Hasidim looked toward Chortkiv; Vizhnitzer Hasidim toward Vyzhnytsia; and other Skala residents identified with centers such as Husiatyn, Ottynia, Horodenka and—if the memorial book’s Yiddish spelling is read correctly—Kopychyntsi. The book’s account names [the Vizhnitzer Hasidim](/communities/skala/records/mention_d867f573cdfee8684cb7f3a0), [the Chartkover Hasidim](/communities/skala/records/mention_3b41da0d581a0d99d8829cd3), [the Husiatiner Hasidim](/communities/skala/records/mention_87ce796a182d6976ca99c027), [the Atinyer Hasidim](/communities/skala/records/mention_8411953c6d119203898c9b52), [the Horodenkover Hasidim](/communities/skala/records/mention_7fcb51f60ae34bc18323e6da), and [the Kopychyntsi Hasidim](/communities/skala/records/mention_8290966e1dd076d7e97f19f2). The last identification is uncertain: the OCR form may be corrupt, so it should not be treated as a settled spelling.

The wider record helps explain why a small town could contain so many currents. Hasidic dynasties spread through Galicia and neighboring regions, drawing followers to a rebbe while establishing local institutions far from his court. Chortkiv’s dynasty, for example, became one of Galicia’s major Hasidic groups; Vizhnitz likewise developed a network of branches and centers. These broader histories provide context, not proof of what any particular Skala resident believed. The Yizkor book’s list is a local memory of affiliations, not a census of membership.

## The kloiz: a local center of belonging

A kloiz was more than a place to pray. It could gather people around a shared Hasidic allegiance, sustain daily worship and study, and give a recognizable shape to neighborhood religious life. Skala’s named institutions included [the Chortkover Kloiz](/communities/skala/records/mention_4478bc9017d1cbc609f17f2f), [the Chartkover kloiz](/communities/skala/records/mention_f0c6c195ae5b1e30267e350c), [the Stryshaver kloiz](/communities/skala/records/mention_73a52f5f537ae3d85f73e1eb), [the Vizhnitzer kloiz](/communities/skala/records/mention_5236fb5fa814b4aa27c9fdb9), and [the Otinyer kloiz](/communities/skala/records/mention_49961228342f19d43505478d). The different spellings—“Chortkover” and “Chartkover”—appear in the supplied records; they refer to the same local Hasidic affiliation, not necessarily to separate groups.

The book makes the institutions vivid by naming the people who served them. [Lazer Shamash](/communities/skala/records/mention_a678a34a8fb7249f838c9aad) and [Shlomo Peretz](/communities/skala/records/mention_a9dfa73ddc89ea374cba5a9a) worked at the Chartkover kloiz; [Berl Shamash](/communities/skala/records/mention_4ff9d0b1b52f13229190cd75) served the Stryshaver kloiz; [Yossel Shamash](/communities/skala/records/mention_9f0593b2e34a228ea1f6f513) the Vizhnitzer; and [Uri Shamash](/communities/skala/records/mention_ff7ea524218b627ef4f81bb9) the Otinyer. The title *shamash* identifies a synagogue attendant, but the surviving notes do not spell out each man’s precise duties. Their names nevertheless preserve the human framework behind the institutions: places of prayer depended on people who kept them functioning.

The book also remembers [Abraham Eli Shamash](/communities/skala/records/mention_79da23177efddc33e98f914d), respected for his knowledge of the town’s graves, and links him to [the synagogue](/communities/skala/records/mention_f0fcd5a8602f5b49c8499f97). It names Aaron Shamash in connection with [the beit midrash](/communities/skala/records/mention_20ba216c82527779374cb4f4), and recalls [Itzik’s kloiz](/communities/skala/records/mention_469349efaad6fa80f99addf5) as another place where residents prayed. These references distinguish several kinds of communal space, but the surviving evidence does not give a complete map of where they stood or how their congregations overlapped.

## Rabbis, learning and religious authority

Skala’s religious life also rested on local rabbinic leadership. The memorial book recalls [Abraham Drimer](/communities/skala/records/mention_c5acfedc7b2e72cb945ea6a6) as rabbi of the Vizhnitz Hasidim and a noted scholar. It also remembers [Shlomo Drimer](/communities/skala/records/mention_8be812c953a526f1af4c2d1f), rabbi in Skala for many years and author of *Beit Shlomo* ([the work](/communities/skala/records/mention_698bacf8588ef8a98c867783)). These are different kinds of authority: the rebbe, whose court stood elsewhere, and the rabbi who taught and served people in Skala.

For the Chartkover group, the memorial book records that [Yehuda Binyamin Loyfer](/communities/skala/records/mention_cc36c4687fb2714d138fbca7) was brought from [Berezhany](/communities/skala/records/mention_7940399b2e310b9a1ac77ca8) as a dayan, or rabbinical judge. That detail suggests that the Hasidic groups could actively recruit religious leadership rather than simply inherit whatever communal services were already available. The book separately says that Skala had two rabbis associated with its opposing Hasidic groups, as well as rabbinical arbiters, ritual slaughterers, supervisors and sextons. It does not make clear that every named rabbi held the same office at the same time, so the surviving accounts should not be compressed into a single fixed roster.

Other local testimony describes a wider texture of observance: study in the beit midrash, children’s religious instruction, Sabbath practice and the adaptations families made amid poverty. That setting matters. A kloiz was one part of a religious world that also included homes, schools, the cemetery, communal services and travel to the rebbe. Local recollections also describe Skala residents consulting distant rebbes about family and business questions—a reminder that the town’s religious life was connected to centers beyond its streets.

## Local diversity and the limits of the record

The memorial book emphasizes Hasidic groups, but its own account leaves room for difference. Not every observant Jew followed a rebbe; some Skala Jews were non-Hasidic, and others were less committed to Hasidic leadership. The JewishGen KehilaLinks account likewise distinguishes between Hasidic and non-Hasidic residents and describes the Chortkover and Vizhnitzer groups as especially prominent. It also notes that the Drimmer family served Vizhnitz adherents over many generations. Because that account draws in part on the same memorial traditions, it is useful for detail but not independent confirmation of them.

Independent records add context rather than a second eyewitness account of the kloizn. Yad Vashem’s place entry identifies the town under the historical Polish name Skala and records 1,555 Jewish residents among 4,017 inhabitants in the 1921 census; it does not document Skala’s individual Hasidic institutions. Its changing country labels also reflect the region’s shifting political borders. A history of Chortkiv’s dynasty places the Chortkover movement within the broader Ruzhin Hasidic family and describes its substantial following in Galicia. Those sources help locate Skala within a larger Jewish and regional landscape, but they do not verify the memorial book’s particular list of attendants, rabbis or kloizn.

The surviving evidence is thus uneven: rich in remembered names and institutional labels, thinner on exact dates, membership and the buildings themselves. The [Skala Jewish community](/communities/skala/records/mention_4d24297290f1a4fed1e56c40) was not simply a collection of branches of distant courts. Each local prayer house gave its adherents a place to meet, learn and maintain a distinct communal rhythm. The remembered shamashim, rabbis and worshippers make that local life legible, even as many questions remain—especially about the precise location of the kloizn, the identification of the Kopychyntsi group, and the extent to which different congregations shared communal services.
